newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila tells Beijing of concern over Spratly ships.
newsitem.headline: Manila tells Beijing of concern over Spratly ships.

text.p: The Philippines told China on Wednesday it was concerned about the sighting of three Chinese warships near areas claimed by Manila in the Spratly Islands and said it would do everything to protect its territory.
Delia Menez Rosal, head of the Asia-Pacific desk at the Foreign Office, met Chinese ambassador Guan Dingming and told him of Manila's concern, officials said.
Rosal told reporters Guan said he knew of the incident only from newspaper reports and that China had no intention of doing anything to mar relations with the Philippines.
Manila newspapers on Wednesday carried Air Force pictures of two of the ships on their front pages.
The Spratlys are a cluster of 190 potentially oil-rich but largely barren isles, reefs and shoals claimed wholly or in part by China, the Philippines, Vietnam, Taiwan, Malaysia and Brunei.

President Fidel Ramos said that besides issuing a diplomatic protest, "our various action agencies are also alerted to make sure that the territorial integrity and the national sovereignty of the Philippines are properly and effectively protected."
"I would like to assure everyone that we are not leaving any stone unturned to protect our citizens as well as our territory," Ramos said at his weekly news conference.
Ramos said he was awaiting reports from both sides before filing the protest.
"You are in an area where the boundary is not well defined and each side has its own version. Let us look at them first," he added.

A government statement on Tuesday said three Chinese Navy ships of the frigate type, accompanied by four fishing boats, were seen last weekend near Kota and Panata islands, which are claimed by Manila. Reconnaissance aircraft also discovered a new hut-like structure built over a reef near Kota, it said.
Philippine Air Force planes flying over the area since the ships were sighted reported that the vessels were still there on Wednesday, a senior military officer said.
Vietnam's foreign ministry, in a statement on Wednesday, called for calm over the issue.

It said Vietnam had no new information on reports of an apparent increase in Chinese military surveillance around the Spratly islands. But it called on regional claimants to the area not to complicate matters by resorting to force.
Philippine Defence Secretary Renato de Villa said the government did not know what the Chinese vessels were doing in the area.
"They are armed vessels ... but what is of deep concern to us is they are quite close to two of the islands that we have occupied," de Villa told reporters.

Tension flared between the Philippines and China in 1995 when Manila accused the Chinese of building what it said looked like naval support structures on Mischief Reef. Beijing said they were shelters for fishermen and has refused to dismantle them.
